claim: A genome-wide siRNA screen was used to molecularly identify ASOR/PAORAC.
source: We now used a genome-wide siRNA screen to molecularly identify the widely expressed acid-sensitive outwardly-rectifying anion channel PAORAC/ASOR.
evidence: The manuscript describes performing a genome-wide siRNA screen as the method used to identify TMEM206.

claim: ASOR is formed by TMEM206 proteins.
source: ASOR is formed by TMEM206 proteins which display two transmembrane domains (TMs) and are expressed at the plasma membrane.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from screening, knockout, and rescue experiments demonstrating TMEM206 forms ASOR.

claim: TMEM206 proteins display two transmembrane domains.
source: ASOR is formed by TMEM206 proteins which display two transmembrane domains (TMs) and are expressed at the plasma membrane.
evidence: The manuscript presents hydropathy analysis and topology experiments supporting two transmembrane domains.

claim: TMEM206 proteins are expressed at the plasma membrane.
source: ASOR is formed by TMEM206 proteins which display two transmembrane domains (TMs) and are expressed at the plasma membrane.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunofluorescence data showing plasma membrane localization.

claim: Ion permeation-changing mutations along the length of TM2 and at the end of TM1 suggest that these segments line ASOR's pore.
source: Ion permeation-changing mutations along the length of TM2 and at the end of TM1 suggest that these segments line ASOR's pore.
evidence: The manuscript presents mutagenesis data showing changes in ion selectivity and permeability.

claim: TMEM206 does not belong to a gene family.
source: While not belonging to a gene family, TMEM206 has orthologs in probably all vertebrates.
evidence: The manuscript states TMEM206 lacks paralogs within species based on sequence analysis.

claim: TMEM206 has orthologs in probably all vertebrates.
source: While not belonging to a gene family, TMEM206 has orthologs in probably all vertebrates.
evidence: The manuscript presents phylogenetic analysis and functional data from multiple vertebrate orthologs.

claim: Currents from evolutionarily distant TMEM206 orthologs share activation by protons.
source: Currents from evolutionarily distant orthologs share activation by protons, a feature essential for ASOR's role in acid-induced cell death.
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data from multiple vertebrate orthologs showing acid activation.

claim: Activation by protons is essential for ASOR's role in acid-induced cell death.
source: Currents from evolutionarily distant orthologs share activation by protons, a feature essential for ASOR's role in acid-induced cell death.
evidence: The manuscript presents cell death assays showing TMEM206 knockout protects against acid-induced cell death.

claim: TMEM206 defines a novel class of ion channels.
source: TMEM206 defines a novel class of ion channels.
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates TMEM206 lacks homology to known channel families and has unique structural features.

claim: Chloride is the most abundant anion in animals.
source: Chloride is by far the most abundant anion in animals.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ion composition in animals.

claim: Chloride concentration can vary substantially between the extracellular space, the cytoplasm and various intracellular organelles.
source: Its concentration can vary substantially between the extracellular space, the cytoplasm and various intracellular organelles, resulting in concentration gradients across membranes separating these compartments.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about chloride distribution in cells.

claim: Chloride channels fulfill a broad range of biological functions, including the homeostasis of cell volume, vesicular acidification, transepithelial transport and cellular signaling.
source: Chloride channels fulfill a broad range of biological functions, including the homeostasis of cell volume, vesicular acidification, transepithelial transport and cellular signaling (Jentsch and Pusch, 2018; Jentsch et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Chloride channels are molecularly and structurally very diverse and lack a defining 'signature' pattern.
source: Chloride channels are molecularly and structurally very diverse and lack a defining 'signature' pattern.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the diversity of chloride channel families.

claim: More than six unrelated Cl- channel families are known.
source: More than six unrelated Cl- channel families are known, prominently including voltage-regulated CLC channels (Jentsch and Pusch, 2018; Jentsch et al., 1990), bestrophin (Hartzell et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2002) and TMEM16 (Caputo et al., 2008; Schroeder et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2008) Ca2+-activated Cl- channels, as well as LRRC8/VRAC volume-regulated anion channels (Qiu et al., 2014; Voss et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Several Cl- currents biophysically characterized in mammalian cells still lack molecular correlates.
source: However, several Cl- currents biophysically characterized in mammalian cells still lack molecular correlates, severely hindering the elucidation of their cellular and organismal functions.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: ASOR is a widely expressed, strongly outwardly-rectifying plasma membrane Cl- current that is detectable only upon marked extracellular acidification.
source: We set out to identify the protein(s) mediating a widely expressed, strongly outwardly-rectifying plasma membrane Cl- current ICl,H that is detectable only upon marked extracellular acidification and which may play a role in acid-induced cell death (Auzanneau et al., 2003; Capurro et al., 2015; Lambert and Oberwinkler, 2005; Sato-Numata et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature describing ASOR properties.

claim: ASOR may play a role in acid-induced cell death.
source: We set out to identify the protein(s) mediating a widely expressed, strongly outwardly-rectifying plasma membrane Cl- current ICl,H that is detectable only upon marked extracellular acidification and which may play a role in acid-induced cell death (Auzanneau et al., 2003; Capurro et al., 2015; Lambert and Oberwinkler, 2005; Sato-Numata et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and later confirmed by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: At room temperature, ASOR currents are only observable when external pH drops below 5.5.
source: At room temperature, ASOR currents are only observable when external pH (pHo) drops below 5.5, but the threshold of activation shifts to ~6.0 at 37°C (Sato-Numata et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The threshold of ASOR activation shifts to ~6.0 at 37°C.
source: At room temperature, ASOR currents are only observable when external pH (pHo) drops below 5.5, but the threshold of activation shifts to ~6.0 at 37°C (Sato-Numata et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Analysis of the steep pH-dependence suggests that 3–4 protons are required to open the ASOR channel.
source: Analysis of the steep pH-dependence suggests that 3–4 protons are required to open the channel (Capurro et al., 2015; Lambert and Oberwinkler, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ASOR currents are strongly outwardly rectifying with almost no currents being observable at negative-inside voltages.
source: ASOR currents are strongly outwardly rectifying with almost no currents being observable at negative-inside voltages.
evidence: This is a well-established property of ASOR from prior literature and confirmed by data in this manuscript.

claim: ASOR rectification results both from voltage-dependent gating that operates on a 100 ms time scale and from an outwardly-rectifying single channel conductance.
source: This rectification results both from voltage-dependent gating that operates on a 100 ms time scale and from an outwardly-rectifying single channel conductance (Lambert and Oberwinkler, 2005) (although others described that single ASOR channels are not rectifying, for example Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature, with a note about conflicting reports.

claim: ASOR currents display an SCN->I->NO3->Br->Cl- permeability sequence.
source: ASOR currents (ICl,H) display an SCN->I->NO3->Br->Cl- permeability sequence.
evidence: This is a known property from prior literature and confirmed by data in this manuscript.

claim: ASOR can be blocked by DIDS and niflumic acid.
source: The channel can be blocked by various Cl- transport inhibitors such as DIDS (4,4'-diisothiocyano-2,2'-stilbenedisulfonic acid) and niflumic acid (Capurro et al., 2015; Lambert and Oberwinkler, 2005) and by other compounds such as phloretin (Wang et al., 2007) and pregnenolone sulfate (PS) (Drews et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and confirmed by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: ASOR can be blocked by phloretin and pregnenolone sulfate.
source: The channel can be blocked by various Cl- transport inhibitors such as DIDS (4,4'-diisothiocyano-2,2'-stilbenedisulfonic acid) and niflumic acid (Capurro et al., 2015; Lambert and Oberwinkler, 2005) and by other compounds such as phloretin (Wang et al., 2007) and pregnenolone sulfate (PS) (Drews et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and confirmed by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: None of the ASOR inhibitors is specific for ASOR.
source: However, none of these inhibitors is specific for ASOR.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of available pharmacological tools.

claim: ICl,H currents have been observed in every investigated mammalian cell type.
source: The observation of ICl,H currents in every investigated mammalian cell type (Auzanneau et al., 2003; Capurro et al., 2015; Fu et al., 2013; Lambert and Oberwinkler, 2005; Ma et al., 2008; Nobles et al., 2004; Sato-Numata et al., 2013; Valinsky et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2007; Yamamoto and Ehara, 2006) suggests that ASOR may be expressed in all tissues.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The wide expression pattern of ASOR suggests that this channel has important physiological functions.
source: Such a wide expression pattern indicates that this channel has important physiological functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed expression pattern.

claim: Only few mammalian cells are physiologically exposed to an extracellular pH that is acidic enough to open ASOR.
source: However, only few mammalian cells are physiologically exposed to an extracellular pH that is acidic enough to open ASOR.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of physiological pH values in different tissues.

claim: ASOR may play a role in pathologies such as cancer or ischemic stroke in which pHo can drop to pH 6.5 or below.
source: It was therefore proposed (Wang et al., 2007) that the channel rather plays a role in pathologies such as cancer or ischemic stroke in which pHo can drop to pH 6.5 or below (Gillies et al., 2018; Kato et al., 2013; Nedergaard et al., 1991; Thews and Riemann, 2019; Xiong et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ASOR inhibitors blunted cell swelling and cell death provoked by prolonged exposure to acidic pHo.
source: Indeed, ASOR inhibitors blunted cell swelling and cell death provoked by prolonged exposure to acidic pHo (Sato-Numata et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2007), suggesting that ASOR-mediated chloride influx may worsen the outcome of ischemic stroke.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ASOR-mediated chloride influx may worsen the outcome of ischemic stroke.
source: Indeed, ASOR inhibitors blunted cell swelling and cell death provoked by prolonged exposure to acidic pHo (Sato-Numata et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2007), suggesting that ASOR-mediated chloride influx may worsen the outcome of ischemic stroke.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited studies and later confirmed by data in this manuscript.

claim: ASOR might be present in intracellular compartments such as lysosomes where it would be exposed to an appropriate acidic pH.
source: Alternatively, ASOR might not only be present at the plasma membrane, but also in intracellular compartments such as lysosomes where it would be exposed to an appropriate acidic pH (Lambert and Oberwinkler, 2005).
evidence: This is a hypothesis cited from prior literature.

claim: LRRC8/VRAC anion channels and ClC-3 Cl-/H+ exchangers have been excluded as candidates for ASOR.
source: The molecular identity of ASOR had remained unknown, with several candidates such as LRRC8/VRAC anion channels or ClC-3 Cl-/H+ exchangers having been excluded previously (Lambert and Oberwinkler, 2005; Sato-Numata et al., 2016; Sato-Numata et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TMEM206 was the top hit in the genome-wide siRNA screen.
source: The top hit was TMEM206, a so far uncharacterized membrane protein (Figure 1D).
evidence: Figure 1D shows the distribution of Z-scores with TMEM206 as the top hit.

claim: TMEM206 is a so far uncharacterized membrane protein.
source: The top hit was TMEM206, a so far uncharacterized membrane protein (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a statement about the prior state of knowledge regarding TMEM206.

claim: The wide tissue expression pattern of TMEM206 agrees with the finding that ICl,H has been found in every cell studied so far.
source: The wide tissue expression pattern of TMEM206 indicated by public databases (Figure 1E) agreed with the finding that ICl,H has been found in every cell studied so far (Auzanneau et al., 2003; Capurro et al., 2015; Fu et al., 2013; Lambert and Oberwinkler, 2005; Ma et al., 2008; Nobles et al., 2004; Sato-Numata et al., 2013; Valinsky et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by expression data from public databases (Figure 1E) and citations to prior literature.

claim: TMEM206 has orthologs in vertebrates and in the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii.
source: TMEM206 has orthologs in vertebrates and in the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii (acorn worm) (Figure 1F), but there are no homologs in simpler animals or other kingdoms of life.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: There are no TMEM206 homologs in simpler animals or other kingdoms of life.
source: TMEM206 has orthologs in vertebrates and in the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii (acorn worm) (Figure 1F), but there are no homologs in simpler animals or other kingdoms of life.
evidence: This is based on sequence database searches.

claim: TMEM206 does not form a gene family because it lacks paralogs within the same species.
source: In contrast to many other ion channels, TMEM206 does not form a gene family because it lacks paralogs within the same species (i.e. it is a 'single gene').
evidence: This is based on sequence database searches.

claim: A significant fraction of GFP-tagged human TMEM206 was found at the plasma membrane after transfection into HeLa cells.
source: After transfection of GFP-tagged human TMEM206 (hTMEM206) into HeLa cells a significant fraction of the protein was found at the plasma membrane (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TMEM206 appeared to be expressed in intracellular membranes, which might result from heterologous overexpression.
source: Additionally, TMEM206 appeared to be expressed in intracellular membranes, which, however, might result from heterologous overexpression.
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence with a cautionary interpretation.

claim: Hydropathy analysis suggested the presence of two transmembrane spans in TMEM206.
source: Hydropathy analysis suggested the presence of two transmembrane spans (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by hydropathy analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Detection of both N- or C-terminally added GFP required permeabilization of the plasma membrane.
source: Detection of both N- or C-terminally added GFP required permeabilization of the plasma membrane (Figure 2C,D), suggesting that both the amino- and the carboxy-terminus of TMEM206 face the cytosol.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Both the amino- and the carboxy-terminus of TMEM206 face the cytosol.
source: Detection of both N- or C-terminally added GFP required permeabilization of the plasma membrane (Figure 2C,D), suggesting that both the amino- and the carboxy-terminus of TMEM206 face the cytosol.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunofluorescence data requiring permeabilization.

claim: A cytosolic localization of the N-terminus is supported by phosphorylation of the amino-terminus of human and rodent TMEM206.
source: A cytosolic localization of the N-terminus is further supported by public databases showing that the amino-terminus of human and rodent TMEM206 can be phosphorylated (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data from public databases.

claim: An extracellular localization of the TM1-TM2 stretch was suggested by immunofluorescent detection of an HA-epitope inserted at position 271 in non-permeabilized cells.
source: An extracellular localization of the TM1-TM2 stretch was suggested by the immunofluorescent detection in non-permeabilized cells of an HA-epitope inserted at position 271 (Figure 2E,G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The TM1-TM2 stretch is glycosylated, supporting its extracellular localization.
source: The observation that this stretch is glycosylated further supports its extracellular localization (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by deglycosylation experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The TM1-TM2 stretch displays consensus sites for N-linked glycosylation at N148, N155, N162, N190.
source: Only this segment displays consensus sites (N148, N155, N162, N190) for N-linked glycosylation (Figure 2G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and shown in figures.

claim: At least one of the N-linked glycosylation sites (N148, N155, N162, N190) is used.
source: Deglycosylation of WT and mutant TMEM206(Δglyc), in which all four consensus sites were eliminated, demonstrated that at least one of these sites are used (Figure 2F) and hence face the lumen of the ER during biogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by deglycosylation experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Both N- and C-termini of TMEM206 reside in the cytosol, whereas the TM1-TM2 loop faces the extracellular space.
source: We conclude that both N- and C-termini of TMEM206 reside in the cytosol, whereas the TM1-TM2 loop faces the extracellular space (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple topology experiments.

claim: Overexpression of human TMEM206 in HEK cells increased acid-activated Cl- currents about 10-fold.
source: Overexpression of human TMEM206 in HEK cells increased acid-activated Cl- currents about 10-fold (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Addition of GFP to either the amino- or carboxy-terminus of TMEM206 only moderately decreased current amplitudes compared to the untagged construct.
source: Addition of GFP to either the amino- or carboxy-terminus of TMEM206 only moderately decreased current amplitudes compared to the untagged construct (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Currents from overexpressed hTMEM206 resembled native ICl,H.
source: Currents from overexpressed hTMEM206, irrespective of whether fused to GFP, resembled native ICl,H.
evidence: This is based on comparison of biophysical properties.

claim: None of the clonal HEK or HeLa KO cell lines displayed measurable ICl,H currents.
source: None of the clonal HEK or HeLa KO cell lines displayed measurable ICl,H currents (Figure 3C–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 3C-E and supplement.

claim: TMEM206 is an indispensable component of ASOR.
source: Hence, TMEM206 is an indispensable component of ASOR.
evidence: This is concluded from knockout experiments showing complete loss of ASOR currents.

claim: Transfection of hTMEM206 rescued ICl,H currents of TMEM206−/− HEK and HeLa cells.
source: Transfection of hTMEM206 rescued ICl,H currents of TMEM206−/− (KO) HEK and HeLa cells (Figure 3F–H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing rescue of currents.

claim: Current characteristics did not differ between transfected WT or KO cells.
source: Current characteristics did not differ between transfected WT or KO cells (Figure 3A,F).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of electrophysiological data.

claim: Currents of overexpressed hTMEM206 showed the typical outward-rectification and activation kinetics of ASOR after depolarizing voltage steps.
source: Currents of overexpressed hTMEM206 (measured at acidic pHo) showed the typical outward-rectification and activation kinetics of ASOR (Capurro et al., 2015; Lambert and Oberwinkler, 2005; Wang et al., 2007) after depolarizing voltage steps (Figure 3C,F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data and comparison to cited literature.

claim: The pHo-dependence of native ICl,H was indistinguishable from that of TMEM206-transfected KO HEK cells.
source: The pHo-dependence of native ICl,H was indistinguishable from that of TMEM206-transfected KO HEK cells (Figure 3I,H).
evidence: This is supported by pH-response curves shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The extent of acidification needed for half-activation of ICl,H is pHo ~5.3.
source: The extent of acidification needed for half-activation of ICl,H (pHo ~5.3) agrees with previous studies (Capurro et al., 2015; Lambert and Oberwinkler, 2005; Sato-Numata et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by pH-response data and citations to prior literature.

claim: Measurements of reversal potentials of hTMEM206-transfected cells revealed a SCN->I->NO3->Br->Cl- permeability sequence.
source: Measurements of reversal potentials of hTMEM206-transfected cells (Figure 4A,B) revealed a SCN->I->NO3->Br->Cl- permeability sequence that is typical for ASOR (Capurro et al., 2015; Lambert and Oberwinkler, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by reversal potential measurements shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Replacement of extracellular Cl- by either gluconate- or SO42- abolished both outward and inward currents.
source: Replacement of extracellular Cl- by either gluconate- (Figure 4C) or SO42- (Figure 4D) not only abolished outward, but also inward currents which are carried by anion efflux.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: Gluconate- and SO42- block the outward movement of Cl- through ASOR/TMEM206 channels.
source: Since we had replaced extracellular, but not intracellular Cl-, these observations suggest that gluconate- and SO42- (or HSO4-, a minor species with which SO42- is at equilibrium and whose abundance will be increased by the acidic pH) block the outward movement of Cl- through ASOR/TMEM206 channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both inward and outward currents are abolished.

claim: ASOR may require activation by extracellular chloride.
source: Alternatively, ASOR may require activation by extracellular chloride.
evidence: This is proposed as an alternative explanation for the loss of currents without extracellular chloride.

claim: Acid-activated currents from overexpressed TMEM206 were efficiently blocked by DIDS, niflumic acid, and pregnenolone sulfate.
source: Acid-activated currents from overexpressed TMEM206 were efficiently blocked by DIDS, niflumic acid, and pregnenolone sulfate (PS, Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figures 4E-H.

claim: The block by PS was fast and reversible.
source: As described for native ICl,H (Drews et al., 2014), the block by PS was fast and reversible (Figure 4F) and affected both outward and inward currents (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figures 4F and 4G.

claim: Overexpressed TMEM206 shares all essential properties with native ASOR currents.
source: We conclude that overexpressed TMEM206 shares all essential properties with native ASOR currents (ICl,H).
evidence: This is concluded from comparison of biophysical and pharmacological properties.

claim: All plasma-membrane expressed TMEM206 orthologs mediated robust acid-activated outwardly rectifying ICl,H currents.
source: Except for the evolutionarily distant hemichordate protein, which was retained in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), all orthologs were expressed at the plasma membrane (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). All plasma-membrane expressed orthologs mediated robust acid-activated outwardly rectifying ICl,H currents (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data from multiple orthologs shown in Figures 5A and 5C.

claim: The hemichordate TMEM206 protein was retained in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Except for the evolutionarily distant hemichordate protein, which was retained in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), all orthologs were expressed at the plasma membrane (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: TMEM206 from Anolis carolinensis mediated outwardly-rectifying currents already at pHo 7.4.
source: Strikingly, TMEM206 from the reptile Anolis carolinensis mediated outwardly-rectifying currents already at pHo 7.4. These currents were further steeply activated when pHo dropped below 6 (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 5A-D.

claim: Currents from all orthologs activated at a threshold of ~pHo 6.
source: Whereas currents from all orthologs activated at a threshold of ~pHo 6, their currents decreased differently at pHo <5 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by pH-response curves shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The current decrease at more acidic pH questions the reliability of determining Hill coefficients for the activation of ASOR by H+ ions.
source: The current decrease at more acidic pH questions the reliability of determining Hill coefficients for the activation of ASOR by H+ ions (Capurro et al., 2015; Lambert and Oberwinkler, 2005; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed current decrease at very acidic pH.

claim: All TMEM206 orthologs displayed the same Cl- permeability.
source: Whereas all orthologs displayed the same Cl- permeability (Figure 5E,I), the mammalian ASORs (human and naked mole-rat) showed a higher iodide/chloride permeability ratio than their chicken, anole and zebrafish orthologs (Figure 5F,I).
evidence: This is supported by reversal potential measurements shown in Figures 5E and 5I.

claim: The mammalian ASORs showed a higher iodide/chloride permeability ratio than their chicken, anole and zebrafish orthologs.
source: Whereas all orthologs displayed the same Cl- permeability (Figure 5E,I), the mammalian ASORs (human and naked mole-rat) showed a higher iodide/chloride permeability ratio than their chicken, anole and zebrafish orthologs (Figure 5F,I).
evidence: This is supported by reversal potential measurements shown in Figures 5F and 5I.

claim: ASORs from green anole and zebrafish displayed a significant SO42- permeability which was undetectable with the other tested orthologs.
source: ASORs from green anole and zebrafish displayed a significant SO42- (or HSO4-) permeability which was undetectable with the other tested orthologs (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: This is supported by reversal potential and current measurements shown in Figures 5G-I.

claim: All vertebrate TMEM206 proteins mediate ASOR currents and participate in forming its ion-selective pore.
source: These results suggest that all vertebrate TMEM206 proteins mediate ASOR currents and participate in forming its ion-selective pore.
evidence: This is concluded from the functional and selectivity data from multiple orthologs.

claim: MTSES lacks significant effects on human WT TMEM206 channels.
source: After having ascertained that the cysteine reagent MTSES lacks significant effects on human WT channels (Figure 6A,B), we generated point mutants in which all residues of both hTMEM206 transmembrane spans were singly replaced by cysteines (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments shown in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: All cysteine mutants except L309C and K319C elicited acid-activated ICl,H currents when transfected into TMEM206−/− HEK cells.
source: Except for two mutants in TM2 (L309C and K319C), all constructs elicited acid-activated ICl,H currents when transfected into TMEM206−/− HEK cells (Figure 6B,C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data from cysteine scanning mutagenesis.

claim: Only one mutant in TM1 (L84C) showed a marked response to cysteine modification.
source: Only one mutant in TM1 (L84C) showed a marked response to cysteine modification (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by MTSES modification data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: Application of MTSES to L84C increased currents selectively at negative voltages.
source: Application of MTSES to this mutant, which changes a residue close to the predicted external end of TM1, increased currents selectively at negative voltages (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by MTSES modification data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: TM2 contained a larger number of responsive cysteine-substituted residues than TM1.
source: TM2, which is less hydrophobic than TM1 (Figure 2B) and may form an amphipathic α-helix (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), contained a larger number of responsive cysteine-substituted residues (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by MTSES modification data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: Responsive residues in TM2 were found close to the external end (W304), close to the center (G312), and more towards the cytoplasmic end (L315, A316).
source: These residues were not only found close to the external end of TM2 (W304), but also close to the center (G312) and more towards the cytoplasmic end of TM2 (L315, A316) (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by MTSES modification data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: The effects of MTSES appeared irreversible.
source: Consistent with a covalent modification of cysteine residues, the effects of MTSES appeared irreversible (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by time course data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Several cysteine mutants showed robust outwardly-rectifying currents already at pHo 7.4.
source: Strikingly, several cysteine mutants showed robust outwardly-rectifying currents already at pHo 7.4 (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claim: Cysteine mutants showing currents at pH 7.4 could be further stimulated by exposure to acidic pHo.
source: These could be further stimulated by exposure to acidic pHo (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Some cysteine mutants displayed changed ion selectivity.
source: Of note, some cysteine mutants displayed changed ion selectivity (Figure 7A,B,F–H).
evidence: This is supported by reversal potential measurements shown in Figures 7A, 7B, and 7F-H.

claim: L84C and R87C mutants displayed a small sulfate permeability that was undetectable in WT hTMEM206.
source: Whereas changes in I- permeability were relatively small (most evident for L84C and R87C, Figure 7B,F), the same two mutants in TM1 displayed a small sulfate permeability that was undetectable in WT hTMEM206, allowing us to determine reversal potentials (Figure 7A,B,G–H).
evidence: This is supported by reversal potential measurements shown in Figures 7A, 7B, and 7G-H.

claim: A number of mutants displayed slightly changed iodide permeability.
source: This yielded detectable ICl,H in many cases (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), with a number of mutants displaying slightly changed iodide permeability (Figure 7C,D,F) or marked increases in SO42-/HSO4- conductance (Figure 7C,G–H).
evidence: This is supported by reversal potential measurements shown in Figures 7C, 7D, and 7F.

claim: A number of mutants displayed marked increases in SO42-/HSO4- conductance.
source: This yielded detectable ICl,H in many cases (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), with a number of mutants displaying slightly changed iodide permeability (Figure 7C,D,F) or marked increases in SO42-/HSO4- conductance (Figure 7C,G–H).
evidence: This is supported by reversal potential and current measurements shown in Figures 7C and 7G-H.

claim: Replacement of L315 by negatively charged aspartate introduced a large ~22 mV shift of the reversal potential in NaCl medium.
source: Strikingly, replacement of L315 by negatively charged aspartate introduced a large ~22 mV shift of the reversal potential in NaCl medium (Figure 7D,E), indicative of a loss of anion selectivity.
evidence: This is supported by reversal potential measurements shown in Figures 7D and 7E.

claim: The L315D mutation is indicative of a loss of anion selectivity.
source: Strikingly, replacement of L315 by negatively charged aspartate introduced a large ~22 mV shift of the reversal potential in NaCl medium (Figure 7D,E), indicative of a loss of anion selectivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the large positive shift in reversal potential.

claim: L315 importantly determines pore properties of ASOR.
source: Together with the strong MTSES effects on the L315C mutant (Figure 6A–C) these data suggest that this TM2 residue importantly determines pore properties of ASOR.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined effects of cysteine modification and charge substitution at this position.

claim: With the exception of R87, all functionally important residues identified in TM1 and TM2 are highly conserved.
source: Of note, with the exception of R87, all functionally important residues identified here in TM1 and TM2 are highly conserved (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Residues along the length of TM2 and towards the external end of TM1 may be close to, or line, the pore of ASOR channels.
source: In conclusion, residues along the length of TM2 and towards the external end of TM1 may be close to, or line, the pore of ASOR channels.
evidence: This is concluded from the cysteine scanning and mutagenesis data.

claim: Disruption of TMEM206 partially protected against acid-induced cell death.
source: Indeed, disruption of TMEM206 partially protected against acid-induced cell death (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figures 8A and 8B.

claim: A roughly similar protection was seen with PS in WT but not in TMEM206−/− cells.
source: A roughly similar protection was seen with PS in WT but not in TMEM206−/− cells (Figure 8A,B), suggesting that the effect of PS on cell viability results from its ability to block ASOR (Drews et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in Figures 8A and 8B.

claim: The effect of PS on cell viability results from its ability to block ASOR.
source: A roughly similar protection was seen with PS in WT but not in TMEM206−/− cells (Figure 8A,B), suggesting that the effect of PS on cell viability results from its ability to block ASOR (Drews et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PS protects WT but not TMEM206−/− cells.

claim: ASOR/TMEM206 channels enhance acidotoxicity.
source: In conclusion, ASOR/TMEM206 channels enhance acidotoxicity.
evidence: This is concluded from the cell death assay data.

claim: WT cells initially swelled faster than TMEM206−/− cells when exposed to pHo 4.2.
source: When exposed to pHo 4.2, both WT and TMEM206−/− HEK cells increased their volume within the first three minutes as indicated by increased calcein fluorescence (Figure 8C). Agreeing with the hypothesis (Sato-Numata et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2007) that the parallel opening of ASOR and ASICs (acid-sensitive Na+-channels; Gründer and Pusch, 2015; Waldmann et al., 1997) leads to an electrically coupled influx of osmotically active Na+ and Cl-, WT cells swelled faster than TMEM206−/− cells.
evidence: This is supported by calcein fluorescence data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: WT cells subsequently decreased their volume after initial swelling, whereas TMEM206−/− cells failed to shrink.
source: Whereas WT cells subsequently decreased their volume, TMEM206−/− cells failed to shrink (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by calcein fluorescence data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The ASOR inhibitor pregnenolone sulfate slowed the initial swelling and inhibited the subsequent shrinkage.
source: Likewise, the ASOR inhibitor pregnenolone sulfate (100 µM) (Drews et al., 2014) slowed the initial swelling and inhibited the subsequent shrinkage (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by calcein fluorescence data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The role of ASOR/TMEM206 in acidotoxicity cannot be explained by a sustained volume increase of acid-exposed cells.
source: Hence, contrasting with the conclusion of Wang et al. (2007), our data suggest that the role of ASOR/TMEM206 in acidotoxicity cannot be explained by a sustained volume increase of acid-exposed cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the cell volume measurements showing shrinkage rather than sustained swelling.

claim: TMEM206 is the essential, pore-forming subunit of ASOR.
source: We have identified TMEM206 as essential, pore-forming subunit of ASOR, a widely expressed acid-sensitive outwardly rectifying anion channel.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript based on all experimental data.

claim: TMEM206 proteins constitute the pore of ASOR, probably in a homo-oligomeric complex.
source: TMEM206 proteins constitute the pore of ASOR, probably in a homo-oligomeric complex.
evidence: This is concluded from mutagenesis data showing TMEM206 determines pore properties, with oligomerization inferred from the two-TM topology.

claim: TMEM206/ASOR channels are involved in acid-induced cell death.
source: TMEM206/ASOR channels are involved in acid-induced cell death, but this role in pathology cannot explain its wide and possibly ubiquitous expression across tissues and vertebrate species.
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data.

claim: The role of TMEM206/ASOR in pathology cannot explain its wide and possibly ubiquitous expression across tissues and vertebrate species.
source: TMEM206/ASOR channels are involved in acid-induced cell death, but this role in pathology cannot explain its wide and possibly ubiquitous expression across tissues and vertebrate species.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the evolutionary significance of the channel.

claim: Yang et al. independently identified TMEM206 as integral component of the ASOR channel.
source: Recently, while the present work was being completed, Yang et al. reported on their independent identification and characterization of TMEM206 as integral component of the ASOR channel (which the authors renamed PAC for Proton-Activated Channel) (Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a citation to a parallel independent study.

claim: Yang et al. showed that Tmem206−/− mice showed smaller stroke areas in a middle cerebral artery occlusion model.
source: Intriguingly, these authors showed that Tmem206−/− mice showed smaller stroke areas in a middle cerebral artery occlusion model (Yang et al., 2019), although the previously reported decrease of pHo in the stroke area (down to ~6.4) (Nedergaard et al., 1991) is slightly above the value needed for ASOR activation.
evidence: This is a citation to findings from the parallel study by Yang et al.

claim: Yang et al. found that reaction of I307C with MTSES reduces ASOR currents.
source: In a cysteine modification scan restricted to the extracellular half of TM2, they also found that reaction of I307C with MTSES reduces ASOR currents, and showed that the I307A mutant displayed moderately decreased iodide permeability.
evidence: This is a citation to findings from the parallel study by Yang et al.

claim: Yang et al. showed that the I307A mutant displayed moderately decreased iodide permeability.
source: In a cysteine modification scan restricted to the extracellular half of TM2, they also found that reaction of I307C with MTSES reduces ASOR currents, and showed that the I307A mutant displayed moderately decreased iodide permeability.
evidence: This is a citation to findings from the parallel study by Yang et al.

claim: The findings of Yang et al. agree with the conclusion that the entire TM2 and the extracellular end of TM1 line ASOR's pore in an oligomeric complex.
source: These results agree with our conclusion that the entire TM2 and the extracellular end of TM1 line ASOR's pore in an oligomeric complex.
evidence: This is a comparison of findings from the parallel study to the current manuscript's conclusions.
